analysis.investment_thesis: Aequs is a capital-intensive contract manufacturer with three consecutive years of net losses, negative free cash flow (-₹239 Cr in FY25), and finance costs (₹64 Cr) that already consume virtually all EBITDA (₹57 Cr) — not a business I'd touch. At P/B of 12.85x and EV/EBITDA of 288x, the market is pricing in a turnaround that the fundamentals simply do not support.
key_strengths: High gross margin of 56% suggests some pricing power in niche manufacturing segments
Promoter holding of 59% provides alignment and strategic commitment
Diversified across aerospace, toys, and consumer durables reduces single-sector risk
key_risks: Finance costs (₹64 Cr) consume 112% of EBITDA (₹57 Cr), making profitability nearly impossible at current debt levels
Free cash flow deeply negative at -₹239 Cr in FY25, with capex accelerating to -₹265 Cr and CWIP ballooning to ₹395 Cr — capital destruction cycle
Extreme overvaluation at 1,140x forward P/E and 12.85x P/B with no earnings to justify multiples
red_flags: Three consecutive years of net losses: -₹110 Cr, -₹14 Cr, -₹102 Cr — no earnings trajectory
ROCE of only 1.11% on a capital-heavy asset base of ₹1,903 Cr is economically destructive
Other income swung to -₹6 Cr in FY25 from +₹44 Cr in FY24, masking underlying deterioration
Equity nearly tripled FY23→FY24 (₹279→₹817 Cr) — likely dilutive fundraise to fund loss-making expansion
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aequs is precisely the kind of business I avoid: capital-intensive, loss-making, and priced as if it were a high-quality compounder. ROCE of 1.11% on ₹1,903 Cr in assets is not a business — it's a capital incinerator. The company is pouring money into a heavy capex cycle (₹265 Cr in FY25, CWIP up to ₹395 Cr) while its EBITDA of ₹57 Cr can't even cover its ₹64 Cr interest bill. Free cash flow has never been positive across the three-year window, deteriorating from -₹76 Cr to -₹239 Cr. Revenue growth has also stalled — from ₹965 Cr in FY24 to ₹925 Cr in FY25 — just as capex hit its peak.

There is no durable competitive moat here. Contract manufacturing in toys, cookware, and aerospace parts is commoditized and structurally low-return. The 56% gross margin sounds attractive but operating leverage is clearly absent — a -1.84% operating margin means every rupee of revenue is being consumed before financing costs. At 288x EV/EBITDA, the market is extrapolating a perfect execution of an unproven industrials thesis. I don't pay 288x for anything, let alone a loss-making manufacturer with negative equity returns. This is not my kind of business at any price, and certainly not at this price.
